speaker: LEHRER
text: Good evening from the Shiley Theatre at the University of San Diego, San Diego, California.

speaker: LEHRER
text: I’m Jim Lehrer of the News Hour on PBS.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Welcome to this second 1996 presidential debate between Senator Bob Dole, the Republican nominee, and President Bill Clinton, the Democratic nominee.

speaker: LEHRER
text: It is sponsored by the Commission on Presidential Debates.

speaker: LEHRER
text: We will follow a town-hall type format tonight.

speaker: LEHRER
text: The questions over the next 90 minutes will come from citizens of the greater San Diego area.

speaker: LEHRER
text: They were chosen in the past week by the Gallup organization to represent a rough cross section of voters as to political views, age, gender and other factors.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Each said he or she is undecided about this presidential race.

speaker: LEHRER
text: They were told to come tonight with questions.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Nobody from the debate commission or the two campaigns has any idea what those questions are.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Neither do I.

speaker: LEHRER
text: We will all be hearing them for the first time at the same time.

speaker: LEHRER
text: I met with this group three hours ago, and we spoke only about how it was going to work tonight.

speaker: LEHRER
text: They are sitting in five sections.

speaker: LEHRER
text: I will call on individuals at random, moving from one section to another with each new question, alternating the questions between the two candidates.

speaker: LEHRER
text: My job is to keep things fair and the subjects as clear and as varied as possible.

speaker: LEHRER
text: The rules, drawn by the campaigns, are basically the same as they were for the Hartford and St.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Petersburg debates; 90 second-answers, 60 -second rebuttals, 30-second responses for each question.

speaker: LEHRER
text: The candidates are not allowed to question each other directly.

speaker: LEHRER
text: There will be two-minute opening and closing statements.

speaker: LEHRER
text: The order for this evening was set by coin toss.

speaker: LEHRER
text: We begin now with Senator Dole and his opening statement.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Senator Dole.

speaker: DOLE
text: Thank you very much, Jim.

speaker: DOLE
text: Let me first give you a sports update.

speaker: DOLE
text: The Braves, one; the Cardinals, nothing, early on.

speaker: DOLE
text: I want to thank you and I want to thank everybody here tonight.

speaker: DOLE
text: I want to give a special thanks to my wife Elizabeth, my daughter Robin for their love and support, and thank the people who are listening and watching all over America.

speaker: DOLE
text: In 20 days, you will help decide who will lead this country into the next century.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s an awesome responsibility.

speaker: DOLE
text: And you must ask yourself, do you know enough about the candidates?

speaker: DOLE
text: You should know as much as possible about each of us.

speaker: DOLE
text: Sometimes the views have been distorted.

speaker: DOLE
text: There’s been millions and millions of dollars of negative advertising spent distorting my views.

speaker: DOLE
text: But I hope tonight you will get a better feel of who Bob Dole is and what he’s all about.

speaker: DOLE
text: And I think first you should — I should understand that the question on your mind is do I understand your problem.

speaker: DOLE
text: Would I understand it if it occurred to me, and I might just say I’m from a large family.

speaker: DOLE
text: I got lots of relatives and they’re good, average, middle-class, hardworking Americans.

speaker: DOLE
text: They live all across the country.

speaker: DOLE
text: They’re not all Republicans.

speaker: DOLE
text: Maybe all but one.

speaker: DOLE
text: But in any event, I understand the problems.

speaker: DOLE
text: Whether it’s two parents working because one has to pay the taxes and one has to provide for the family, whether it’s a single parent who just barely pays the pressing bills or whether you’re worried about an education for your children going to the best schools, or whether you’re worried about safe playgrounds, drug-free schools, crime-free schools.

speaker: DOLE
text: This is what this election is all about.

speaker: DOLE
text: And hopefully tonight when we conclude this debate you will have a better understanding and the viewing and listening audience will have a better understanding.

speaker: DOLE
text: Thank you.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President, two minutes, opening statement.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I was going to applaud, too.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Well, thank you, Jim.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And thanks to the people of San Diego for giving us this opportunity to have another discussion about the decision we all face in front of people who will make the decision.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Again, I will say I will do my best to make this a discussion of ideas and issues, not insults.

speaker: CLINTON
text: What really matters is what happens to your future and what happens to our country as we stand on the brink of a new century, a time of extraordinary possibility.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I have a simple philosophy that I tried to follow for the last four years: Do what creates opportunity for all, what reinforces responsibility from all of us, and what will help us build a community where everybody’s got a role to play and a place at the table.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Compared to four years ago, we’re clearly better off.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We’ve got ten and a half million more jobs, the deficit’s been reduced by 60 percent.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Incomes are rising for the first time in a decade, the crime rates, the welfare rolls are falling, we’re putting , 100,000 more police on the street.

speaker: CLINTON
text: 60,000 felons, fugitives and stalkers have been denied handguns.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But that progress is only the beginning.

speaker: CLINTON
text: What we really should focus on tonight is what we still have to do to help the American people make the most of this future that’s out there.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think what really matters is what we can do to build strong families.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Strong families need a strong economy.

speaker: CLINTON
text: To me that means we have to go on and balance this budget while we protect Medicare and Medicaid and education and the environment.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We should give a tax cut, targeted to child rearing and education, to buying a first home and paying for health care.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We ought to help protect our kids from drugs and guns and gangs and tobacco.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We ought to help move a million people from welfare to work and we ought to create the finest education system in the world where every 18-year-old can go on to college and all of our younger children have great educational opportunities.

speaker: CLINTON
text: If we do those things, we can build that bridge to the 21st century.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s what I hope to get to talk about tonight.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Thank you.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Let’s go now to the first question from this section.

speaker: LEHRER
text: For Senator Dole.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes, ma’am.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes.

speaker: LEHRER
text: MS.

speaker: LEHRER
text: McAFEE: Hello, Senator Dole.

speaker: DOLE
text: Hi.

speaker: DOLE
text: MS.

speaker: DOLE
text: McAFEE: My name is Shannon McAfee.

speaker: DOLE
text: I’m a beginning educator in this country, and I really think it’s important what children have to say.

speaker: DOLE
text: They’re still very idealistic.

speaker: DOLE
text: And they — everything they say comes from the heart.

speaker: DOLE
text: I have a quote for you from “If I Were President,” compiled by Peggy Gavin.

speaker: DOLE
text: A sixth grader says, “If I were president, I would think about Abraham Lincoln and George Washington and what they did to make our country great.

speaker: DOLE
text: We should unite the white and black people and people of all cultures.

speaker: DOLE
text: Democrats and Republicans should unite also.

speaker: DOLE
text: We should all come together and think of the best ways to solve the economic problems of our country.

speaker: DOLE
text: “I believe that when we are able to come together and stop fighting amongst ourselves we will get along a lot better.

speaker: DOLE
text: ” These are the ideals and morals that we are teach — we are trying to teach our children in these days.

speaker: DOLE
text: Yet we don’t seem to be practicing them in our government, in anything.

speaker: DOLE
text: If you are president, how will you begin to practice what we are preaching to our children, the future of our nation?

speaker: DOLE
text: Well, I would say first of all, I think, it’s a very good question.

speaker: DOLE
text: I appreciate the quote from the young man.

speaker: DOLE
text: There’s no doubt about it that many American people have lost their faith in government.

speaker: DOLE
text: They see scandals almost on a daily basis.

speaker: DOLE
text: They see ethical problems in the Whitehouse today.

speaker: DOLE
text: They see 900 FBI files, private person, being gathered up by somebody in the Whitehouse.

speaker: DOLE
text: Nobody knows who hired this man.

speaker: DOLE
text: So there’s a great deal of cynicism out there.

speaker: DOLE
text: But I’ve always tried in whatever I’ve done is to bring people together.

speaker: DOLE
text: I said in my acceptance speech in San Diego about two months ago that the exits are clearly marked.

speaker: DOLE
text: If you think the Republican party is some place for you to come if you’re narrow minded or bigoted or don’t like certain people in America, the exits are clearly marked for you to walk out of as I stand here without compromise, because this is the party of Lincoln.

speaker: DOLE
text: I think we have a real obligation, obviously public officials.

speaker: DOLE
text: I’m no longer a public official.

speaker: DOLE
text: I left public life on June the 11th of this year.

speaker: DOLE
text: But it is very important.

speaker: DOLE
text: Young people are looking to us.

speaker: DOLE
text: They’re looking to us for leadership.

speaker: DOLE
text: They’re watching what we do, what we say, what we promise and what we finally deliver.

speaker: DOLE
text: And I would think, it seems to me that there are opportunities here.

speaker: DOLE
text: When I’m President of the United States, I will keep my word.

speaker: DOLE
text: My word is my bond.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President.

speaker: CLINTON
text: One of the reasons that I ran for president, Sandy, is because not just children, a lot of grownups felt that way.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And if you remember four years ago, we had not only rising unemployment, but a lot of rising cynicism.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I had never worked in Washington as an elected official.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It seemed to me that most of the arguments were partisan, Republican, Democrat, left, right, liberal, conservative.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s why I said tonight I’m for opportunity, responsibility and community.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And we’ve gotten some real progress in the last four years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve also done everything I could at every moment of division in this country, after Oklahoma City, when these churches were burned, to bring people together and remind people that we are stronger because of our diversity.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We have to respect one another.

speaker: CLINTON
text: You mentioned Washington and Lincoln.

speaker: CLINTON
text: They were presidents at historic times.

speaker: CLINTON
text: This is an historic time.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s important we go beyond those old partisan arguments and focus on people and their future.

speaker: CLINTON
text: When we do that, instead of shutting the government down over a partisan fight over the budget, we’re a better country and that’s why we’re making progress now.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Senator.

speaker: DOLE
text: Well, bringing people together, again, is obviously a responsibility we all have.

speaker: DOLE
text: I know you do it.

speaker: DOLE
text: Everybody here does it.

speaker: DOLE
text: You do a lot of things nobody knows about.

speaker: DOLE
text: I have a little foundation for the disabled called the Dole Foundation.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’ve raised about $10 million.

speaker: DOLE
text: We don’t talk about it.

speaker: DOLE
text: We try to help people with disabilities.

speaker: DOLE
text: Bring them back into the mainstream of public life.

speaker: DOLE
text: So it seems to me that there’s also a public trust.

speaker: DOLE
text: When you’re the president of the United States, you have a public trust and you have to keep that public trust, as George Washington, as Abraham Lincoln did.

speaker: DOLE
text: And I think now that trust is being violated and it seems to me we ought to face up to it, and the president ought to say tonight that he’s not going to pardon anybody that he was involved in business with who might implicate him later on.

speaker: LEHRER
text: All right.

speaker: LEHRER
text: The next question from this section right here.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Right there in the middle, sir.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes, sir.

speaker: DR. BERKLEY
text: Dr.

speaker: DR. BERKLEY
text: Robert N.

speaker: DR. BERKLEY
text: Berkley.

speaker: DR. BERKLEY
text: I’m a cardiologist from Fallbrook, California.

speaker: DR. BERKLEY
text: Mr.

speaker: DR. BERKLEY
text: President, I would like to know if you would please explain your plans for — in a substantive fashion for addressing the problems with the health care system in our country.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I will.

speaker: CLINTON
text: First of all, let me say what we have done.

speaker: CLINTON
text: In the last four years we’ve worked hard to promote more competition to bring down the rate of inflation in health care costs without eroding health care quality.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The government pays for Medicare and Medicaid, as you know, and that’s very important.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Secondly, we’ve added a million more children to the ranks of the insured through the Medicaid program.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We have protected 25 million people through the passage of the Kennedy-Kassebaum bill that says you can use your health insurance if you change jobs or someone in your family has been sick.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We just recently ended those drive-by deliveries saying people can’t be kicked out of the hospital by insurance companies when they’ve just had babies.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So this is, that’s a good start.

speaker: CLINTON
text: In the next four years, I want to focus on the following things.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Number one, add another million children to the insured ranks through the Medicaid program.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Number two, keep working with the states, as we are now, to add 2.

speaker: CLINTON
text: 2 million more people to the insurance system.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Number three, cover people who are between jobs for up to six months.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That could protect 3 million families, 700,000 kids.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Number four, make sure we protect the integrity with the Medicare program and Medicaid program and not do anything in cutting costs which would cause hundreds of hospitals to close which could have been the case if the 270billion dollar Medicare cut that I vetoed, had been enacted in the law.

speaker: DOLE
text: Well, first, let me say there you go again, Mr.

speaker: DOLE
text: President, talking about a Medicare cut.

speaker: DOLE
text: I have heard you say this time after time.

speaker: DOLE
text: I have heard you say on one TV appearance, “the media made me do it.

speaker: DOLE
text: ” You were trying to defend your cut which was not a cut either, Reduction in the growth of spending.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’ve always had at least 7 percent.

speaker: DOLE
text: You’ve said publicly that it’s now three times the rate of inflation.

speaker: DOLE
text: We ought to cut the growth to twice the rate of inflation.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s about where we are now.

speaker: DOLE
text: So let’s stop talking about cutting Medicare.

speaker: DOLE
text: In my economic plan we increase it 39percent.

speaker: DOLE
text: Don’t forget what he tried to do with health care.

speaker: DOLE
text: 17 new taxes, spend 1.

speaker: DOLE
text: 5 trillion dollars, 50 new bureaucracies.

speaker: DOLE
text: Can you believe that?

speaker: DOLE
text: You couldn’t even have been a cardiologist because he had quotas.

speaker: DOLE
text: You’re a cardiologist, it wouldn’t affect you.

speaker: DOLE
text: But if somebody wanted to be a cardiologist, ten years from now, you’d have to be certain you complied with some of the rules in this extreme medical plan the government was going to take over for all Americans.

speaker: DOLE
text: There are things we can do like the Kassebaum bill.

speaker: DOLE
text: We changed many provisions I authored, cover preexisting conditions, portability, and there are other things we can do.

speaker: DOLE
text: We still need to cover about 20million people and a lot of children.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I don’t have time in 30 seconds to respond to fix all that.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But let me just say the American Hospital Association said that the budget I vetoed could have closed 700 hospitals.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Not me.

speaker: CLINTON
text: On a per-person basis, it did cut way below the rate of inflation in medical costs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But the important thing is what are we going to do now?

speaker: CLINTON
text: We need to help people who are between jobs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We need to cover more kids.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Provide more preventative care.

speaker: CLINTON
text: My balanced budget covers mammograms for ladies, women on Medicare and also gives respite care to the million-plus families who have someone with Alzheimerâ€™s.

speaker: CLINTON
text: These things are paid for in the balanced budget plan.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’ll move us forward.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Next question is for Senator Dole from here.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes, sir.

speaker: MR. MILLIGAN
text: Senator Dole, my name is Jason Milligan, active duty military and small business owner, and my question is: What is your position on closing the gap between military and civilian pay scales?

speaker: DOLE
text: Jason, I appreciate that very much, being a former military man myself.

speaker: DOLE
text: You know, we have 17,000 men and women today wearing our uniform that receive food stamps.

speaker: DOLE
text: It shouldn’t happen in America.

speaker: DOLE
text: We have men and women wearing our uniform in substandard housing.

speaker: DOLE
text: It shouldn’t happen in America.

speaker: DOLE
text: And it’s time we take a look at the pay scales.

speaker: DOLE
text: Did get a 3 percent increase this year, but that’s not enough.

speaker: DOLE
text: If we’re going to ask young men and young women to protect us and defend us around the world, and we’ve had more deployments under this administration than any time in history.

speaker: DOLE
text: Fifty times we deployed troops around the world.

speaker: DOLE
text: Every time you do that you take a risk.

speaker: DOLE
text: Somebody, you know, maybe your son, maybe your grandson, maybe somebody else.

speaker: DOLE
text: But I think anybody who wears a uniform is a great American.

speaker: DOLE
text: Remember Vietnam?

speaker: DOLE
text: Remember when people almost used to walk across the street rather than have a contact with somebody who was in Vietnam?

speaker: DOLE
text: That’s all behind us now, and it should be behind us, and the forgotten war, the Korean War, but I guess I can just answer you very plainly, Jason.

speaker: DOLE
text: Thank you for doing what you’re doing.

speaker: DOLE
text: America owes you a debt of gratitude.

speaker: CLINTON
text: May I ask you a question?

speaker: CLINTON
text: What service are you in?

speaker: MR. MILLIGAN
text: I’m in the United States Navy, sir.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And what kind of small business do you have?

speaker: MR. MILLIGAN
text: I have an Amway business.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Good for you.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let me say, if Senator Dole mentioned this, I just signed a bill that we got through Congress to increase the amount of pay increase we could give for military personnel and to make sure the pay increase this year was above the rate of inflation.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I also presented to the Congress and they adopted a large package of quality-of-life improvements, which are very important.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I spent a lot of time talking to military families as well as military members all over the world and in bases all across the United States, and I became convinced after talking to the families and the personnel in uniform that we needed to not only have the pay raise but we needed to invest more in child care, housing, and other things to support families, especially when there are longer deployments because of the downsizing of the military.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So I, we’re going to do better, and we’ll do better still, but this is a commitment I think that all Americans share without regard to party.

speaker: DOLE
text: I don’t disagree with anything that the President said, except he waited four years to do these things, and my view is it ought to be, it will be done on Day 1.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’ll start working on Day 1 in the Dole- Kemp administration.

speaker: DOLE
text: This is important.

speaker: DOLE
text: We only have ten divisions now.

speaker: DOLE
text: We used to have 18.

speaker: DOLE
text: We had 25 fighter wings.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’re down to 13.

speaker: DOLE
text: We had 536 ships.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’re down to 336 ships.

speaker: DOLE
text: I mean, we’ve cut defense spending too much in the first place.

speaker: DOLE
text: The President told you in ’92 he would cut it 67 billion.

speaker: DOLE
text: He cut 112 billion dollars, so we’re right on the edge right now.

speaker: DOLE
text: But the last thing we ought to do is make those who wear the uniforms sacrifice.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Next question here for President Clinton.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes, ma’am, here on the front row.

speaker: MS. KELLY
text: President Clinton, my name is Cecily Kelly.

speaker: MS. KELLY
text: Yesterday, Yassir Arafat said in Palestine that he thinks the key to success in the Middle East is the commitment of Americans.

speaker: MS. KELLY
text: Would you as President send American troops to Israel or the West Bank as peacekeepers?

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let me just take two seconds of my time because I’m the Commander-in-Chief to respond to one thing that was said.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I propose to spend 1.

speaker: CLINTON
text: 6 trillion dollars on defense between now and the year 2002 and there’s less than 1 percent difference between my budget and the Republican budget on defense.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now, on the Middle East, as you know, I worked very hard for peace in the Middle East.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The agreement between the Palestinians and the Israelis was signed at the White House and the agreement — the peace treaty with Jordan, I was — I went to Jordan to sign that — to be there.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But — and I think the United States can do whatever we reasonably can.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I can say this: I do not believe Yassir Arafat wants us to send troops to the West Bank.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We have never been asked to send troops to the West Bank.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I saw the agreement that Prime Minister Rabin and Yassir Arafat signed on the West Bank.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It had 26 separate maps they had to sign, literally thousands of delineations of who would do what on the West Bank, and I believe if the parties will get together and in a good-faith manner make that agreement, that they’ll be able to do it if we cannot impose a peace on the Middle East.

speaker: CLINTON
text: My position has always been that the job of the United States was to minimize the risks of peace.

speaker: CLINTON
text: You know, if they asked me to be part of some monitoring force — as we are in the Sinai and have been since 1978 — to monitor the peace between Egypt and Israel, frankly, I would have to think about it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I would have to see what they wanted to do, but I don’t believe that will be the request.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think what Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Arafat wants us to do is to make sure that everybody honors the agreements they’ve already made.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s why I brought the leaders to Washington a few days ago.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think they will, and I think we’ll get there.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Don’t be too discouraged.

speaker: DOLE
text: Let me, Jason, come back to you a minute because there is a big difference in the defense budget.

speaker: DOLE
text: We had 7 billion this year and 10 billion more than the president.

speaker: DOLE
text: He puts his money in the outyears, and even if he were re-elected, he’d be gone before anything would happen, and nothing is going to happen.

speaker: DOLE
text: We don’t have modernization now.

speaker: DOLE
text: If we don’t build more B-2 bombers in California and we lost about 500,000 jobs out in California, because of this devastation, these big, big cuts.

speaker: DOLE
text: We had to make cuts.

speaker: DOLE
text: We didn’t have the cuts the president promised he’d make and then he doubled.

speaker: DOLE
text: I think we need to go back and take a look.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’re increasing defense reasonably — not too much, but we are increasing defense some — because we want to be prepared in case somebody here gets called up, Jason.

speaker: DOLE
text: I would say I didn’t hear what Yassir Arafat had to say, but I don’t want to — you know, I think foreign policy, I want to be very careful about, and I’m not here to argue about the President with some ongoing foreign policy matter.

speaker: DOLE
text: What I want the President to do, and I think he may have done it, his last statement, call for an unconditional end of the violence and have the parties keep on talking as they should talk and have a resolution.

speaker: DOLE
text: The last thing we want to do is commit more forces anywhere.

speaker: DOLE
text: But let’s sort of keep this out of politics because it’s pretty dicey right now.

speaker: CLINTON
text: When the change of government occurred in Israel, the people of Israel were saying we don’t want to abandon the peace process.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We want more security.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Then a lot of mutual distrust developed.

speaker: CLINTON
text: A lot of things happened which maybe shouldn’t have happened.

speaker: CLINTON
text: When I asked Yassir Arafat and Prime Minister Netanyahu to come to Washington and got them together and they talked alone for three hours, I was convinced that they had to have a chance to make that peace.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Again, I’d say if they asked us to play some reasonable role, I don’t know how I would respond.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It would depend entirely on what they asked us to do, but the real secret there is for them to abide by the agreements they’ve made and find a way to trust each other, and they’re going to have to spend some time and trust each other.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Prime Minister Rabin gave his life believing that that trust could be materialized, and I still think it can be.

text: Yes sir.

speaker: MR. DELGADO
text: Senator Dole, Oscar Delgado.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Oscar.

speaker: MR. DELGADO
text: Exsmoker for 30 years.

speaker: MR. DELGADO
text: About 30 years ago I was a pack-plus a day man.

speaker: MR. DELGADO
text: Okay?

speaker: MR. DELGADO
text: You mentioned a statement — you said some time ago that you didn’t think nicotine was addictive.

speaker: MR. DELGADO
text: Would you care to — are you still holding to that statement, or do you wish to recant or explain yourself?

speaker: DOLE
text: Oh, that’s very easy.

speaker: DOLE
text: My record going back to 1965 in the Congress, the first vote we had was whether or not you should put a little notice on cigarettes.

speaker: DOLE
text: They may be danger — I voted I for everything since that time.

speaker: DOLE
text: In fact, 1992 we had a bill come before us that all the states had to comply or they’re going to lose certain money.

speaker: DOLE
text: We sent it to the Clinton Administration for implementation, and they waited three and a half years.

speaker: DOLE
text: And during that period about 3,000 young kids every day started smoking.

speaker: DOLE
text: So you add it up.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’s about three million.

speaker: DOLE
text: Not until again in 1996 — I don’t want anybody to smoke.

speaker: DOLE
text: My brother probably died partly because of cigarettes.

speaker: DOLE
text: I was asked a technical question.

speaker: DOLE
text: Are they addictive?

speaker: DOLE
text: Maybe they — they probably are addictive.

speaker: DOLE
text: I don’t know.

speaker: DOLE
text: I’m not a doctor.

speaker: DOLE
text: You shouldn’t smoke.

speaker: DOLE
text: You ought to be glad you quit, Oscar, 30 years.

speaker: DOLE
text: And it seems to me what we need to do is to talk about not only tobacco but drugs, because drug use between 12- and 17-year-olds has doubled in this administration in the last 44 months.

speaker: DOLE
text: Marijuana use is up 141percent.

speaker: DOLE
text: Cocaine use up 160 percent.

speaker: DOLE
text: They’re your kids.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s all happening in this administration because they cut funding and they cut interdiction.

speaker: DOLE
text: When I’m President of the United States, we’re going to use the National Guard and whatever sources we need to stop some of the drugs coming into America.

speaker: DOLE
text: If you stop the drugs, nobody is going to use the drugs; so don’t smoke, don’t drink, don’t use drugs.

speaker: DOLE
text: Just don’t do it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Oscar, the question of what the federal government should do to limit the access of tobacco to young people is one of the biggest differences between Senator Dole and me.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We did propose a regulation six months after I became President under the law he mentioned.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It simply says all these states — it made it illegal for kids to smoke.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now they have to try harder if they want to keep getting federal funds.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Then we took comments, as we always do, and there were tens of thousands of comments as to how we ought to do it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s what drug it out.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Meanwhile, we started the — also in ’93 to look into whether cigarettes were addictive enough for the Federal Food and Drug Administration to ban the ability of cigarette companies to advertise, market and distribute their products to our kids.

speaker: CLINTON
text: No president had ever taken on the tobacco lobby before.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I did.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Senator Dole opposed me.

speaker: CLINTON
text: He went down and made a speech to people who were on his side saying that I did the wrong thing.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think I did the right thing.

speaker: CLINTON
text: On drugs, I have repeatedly said drugs are wrong and illegal and can kill you.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We have strengthened enforcement, and everybody in San Diego knows we strengthened control of the border.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We have done a lot more, and I hope we get a chance to talk about it.

speaker: DOLE
text: Well, they also know if they live in San Diego, Mr.

speaker: DOLE
text: President, if you’re caught with 125 pounds of marijuana or less, you go back to Mexico.

speaker: DOLE
text: You’re not prosecuted.

speaker: DOLE
text: You have a U.

speaker: DOLE
text: attorney here that sends `em back home, so I think that’s pretty important.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’s a lot of marijuana.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’s a big supply.

speaker: DOLE
text: But don’t get into this smoke screen here Oscar.

speaker: DOLE
text: The President in the election year decided I ought to do something, I haven’t done anything on drugs.

speaker: DOLE
text: I’ve been AWOL for 44 months, so let’s take on smoking, see they haven’t even done it.

speaker: DOLE
text: They haven’t said what’s going to happen, whether they’re going to have it declared addictive.

speaker: DOLE
text: Once it’s a drug, does it apply only to teenagers or everybody in America?

speaker: DOLE
text: Nobody should smoke, young or old, but particularly young people should not smoke, but my record is there.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s been there.

speaker: DOLE
text: I’ve voted eight, ten times since 1965.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Next question is for President Clinton.

speaker: LEHRER
text: It comes from right here.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes, sir.

speaker: MR. FLECK
text: President Clinton, my name is Jack Fleck.

speaker: MR. FLECK
text: I’m retired Air Force pilot.

speaker: MR. FLECK
text: Sir, it’s officially forecast that our annual Medicare and Social Security deficits are measured in the trillions of dollars next century.

speaker: MR. FLECK
text: Depending on who you listen to, Social Security will be bankrupted in either 2025 or 2030.

speaker: MR. FLECK
text: I feel this is grossly unfair, especially to our younger generation who are losing faith in the system.

speaker: MR. FLECK
text: My question is this: Assuming you agree that our entitlement programs are on an unsustainable course, what specific reforms do you propose?

speaker: CLINTON
text: First of all, there are two different things.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Social Security and Medicare are entirely different in terms of the financial stabilities.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let’s talk about them separately.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Social Security is stable until, as you pointed out, at least the third decade of the next century.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But we’d like to have a Social Security fund that has about 70 years of life instead of about 30 years of life.

speaker: CLINTON
text: What we have to do is simply to make some adjustments to take account of the fact that the baby boomers, people like me, are bigger in number than the people that went just before us and the people that come just after us.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I think what we’ll plainly do is what we did in 1983 when Senator Dole served, and this is something I think he did a good job on when he served on the Social Security commission and they made some modest changes in Social Security to make sure that it would be alive and well into the 21st century.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And we will do that.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s obvious that there are certain things that have to be done and there are 50 or 60 different options, and a bipartisan commission to take it out of politics, will make recommendations and build support for the people.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Medicare is different.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Medicare needs help now.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I have proposed a budget which would put ten years on the life of the Medicare trust fund.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s more than it’s had a lot of the time in the last years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It would save a lot of money through more managed care, by giving more options, more preventative care and lowering the inflation rate and the prices we’re paying providers without having the kind of big premium increases and out-of-pocket costs that the budget I vetoed would provide.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Then that would give us ten years to do with Medicare what we’re going to do with Social Security; have a bipartisan group look at what we have to do to save it when the baby boomers retire.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But now we can, we ought to pass this budget now and put ten years on it right away so no one has to worry about it.

speaker: DOLE
text: Well again, if you’re somebody thinking about the future, I think it’s fair to say that it’ll be — we’ll work it out.

speaker: DOLE
text: This is a political year, and the President is playing politics with Medicare.

speaker: DOLE
text: After this year is over, we’ll resolve it just as we did with Social Security in `83.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s a nonpartisan commission.

speaker: DOLE
text: Ronald Reagan got together with Tip O’Neill and Howard Baker, two Republicans and one Democrat.

speaker: DOLE
text: They appointed a commission I was on that commission.

speaker: DOLE
text: We resolved, we rescued Social Security.

speaker: DOLE
text: We suggested — I think it has been over a year ago now — we do the same with Medicare, and the White House called it a gimmick.

speaker: DOLE
text: Now last week I guess it was Donna Shalala said well we’ll cut Medicare a hundred billion and appoint a commission.

speaker: DOLE
text: It will probably have to be done by a commission.

speaker: DOLE
text: Take it out of politics.

speaker: DOLE
text: I think if I were a senior citizen I would be a little fed up with all these ads scaring seniors, scaring veterans and scaring students about education.

speaker: DOLE
text: When you don’t have any ideas, you don’t have any agenda, and all you have is fear, that’s all you can use.

speaker: DOLE
text: We have ideas in the Dole-Kemp campaign and we will rescue Medicare as we did Social Security.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Their idea was to have the poorest seniors in the country pay $270 more this year.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Their idea was a budget that the that the American Hospital Association said could close 700 hospitals.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Their idea was to charge everybody more out-of-pocket costs in their budget that I vetoed.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Not in an election year, sir.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I told them in early ’95.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Senator Dole said 30 years ago he was one of 12 people who voted against Medicare and he was proud of it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: A year ago he said, “I was right then.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I knew it wouldn’t work.

speaker: CLINTON
text: ” American seniors have the highest life expectancy in the world.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We need to reform it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Not wreck it.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Next question from here for Senator Dole.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes, ma’am.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Right here.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes.

speaker: MS. GONZALEZ
text: Senator Dole my name is Susan Gonzalez.

speaker: MS. GONZALEZ
text: And I would like to know what you are — what would be your first step in reforming welfare?

speaker: DOLE
text: Well, we’ve taken the first step.

speaker: DOLE
text: Took it three steps, twice we sent welfare reform to the president and he vetoed it.

speaker: DOLE
text: On the third time we sent welfare reform to the president he signed it but announced he would change it next year, and the vice president said they were going to do something else through the line item veto which I’ve never understood, but that’s sort of inside baseball.

speaker: DOLE
text: What we need to do is make certain we try to return people to work.

speaker: DOLE
text: And I’m standing here as someone who, a long time ago as the county attorney in Russell, Kansas, one of our jobs every month was go through all the welfare checks and sign them.

speaker: DOLE
text: And three of those checks were my grandparents’.

speaker: DOLE
text: So I know what it’s like to have to look welfare head-on.

speaker: DOLE
text: Obviously some people are going to need help.

speaker: DOLE
text: This is the United States of America.

speaker: DOLE
text: You’re not going to go without food and you’re not going to go without medical care.

speaker: DOLE
text: This is America.

speaker: DOLE
text: But at the same time, if you want to get off Medicare, get back in the mainstream, we’re going to provide jobs.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’re going to say you have a five-year limit.

speaker: DOLE
text: You can be on welfare.

speaker: DOLE
text: You got two years to look for a job.

speaker: DOLE
text: We provided more money for daycare in the bill that passed the senate, was vetoed, then it came back and the president signed pretty much the same bill.

speaker: DOLE
text: But this is an important issue.

speaker: DOLE
text: I don’t think we ought to be giving welfare payments to illegal immigrants.

speaker: DOLE
text: It puts a heavy burden on a state like — except for emergencies.

speaker: DOLE
text: It puts a heavy burden on a states like California.

speaker: DOLE
text: It costs California taxpayers 3 billion dollars a year.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President Clinton.

speaker: DOLE
text: Let me get out of your way here.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s illegal right now and has been for years for illegal immigrants to get welfare benefits.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let me say that this is one of the most important issues in the world to me.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I started working on welfare reform in 1980 because I was sick of seeing people trapped in a system that was increasingly isolating them and making their kids more vulnerable to get in trouble.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So I’ve been working on it when I was a governor for a long time.

speaker: CLINTON
text: When I became president I used the authority I had in this law to get out from certain federal rules to help states move people to work.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We reduced the welfare rolls by 2 million already.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now, I’ve got a plan with this new welfare reform law to work with the private sector, to give employees specific tax incentives to hire people off welfare, and to do some other things which will create more jobs in the private sector, at least a million, and move more people from welfare to work.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s very important.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I hope we get a chance to talk about this more.

speaker: CLINTON
text: There’s not a more important issue.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I, I still remember a woman that I met ten years ago who said she wanted to get off welfare so her kids could tell, give an answer when they say, “What does your mother do for a job?

speaker: CLINTON
text: ” I met that woman again.

speaker: CLINTON
text: She’s got four kids.

speaker: CLINTON
text: One’s got a good job, one’s studying to be a doctor.

speaker: CLINTON
text: One’s in technical school, one’s an honor student in high school.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I want to make more people like that woman, Lily Harden, so I’ve got a plan to do it, and it’s just beginning.

speaker: DOLE
text: Well another thing we can do.

speaker: DOLE
text: We talk about growth.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’ve got a great economic package which I hope we will discuss later.

speaker: DOLE
text: Across-the-board tax cut.

speaker: DOLE
text: Child credits.

speaker: DOLE
text: $500 per child under 18.

speaker: DOLE
text: Reduce the capital gains rate.

speaker: DOLE
text: Create more jobs and opportunities for people on and off welfare.

speaker: DOLE
text: We have other provisions.

speaker: DOLE
text: Less litigation.

speaker: DOLE
text: The trial lawyers, big supporters of the president.

speaker: DOLE
text: The trial lawyers, of course they like lawsuits, so every time they have a bill that they want vetoed, the president vetoes it for them.

speaker: DOLE
text: We’ve got to understand in America that we’ve got to have growth, create more jobs and more opportunities in the private sector.

speaker: DOLE
text: The president takes credit for all these people off welfare.

speaker: DOLE
text: The governors did that.

speaker: DOLE
text: Federal government doesn’t do that.

speaker: DOLE
text: And the government doesn’t create jobs.

speaker: DOLE
text: They’re created in the private sector.

speaker: LEHRER
text: This section, question?

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes ma’am.

speaker: LEHRER
text: On the back row.

speaker: LEHRER
text: This is for the president.

speaker: MS. JOHNSON
text: Mr.

speaker: MS. JOHNSON
text: President.

speaker: MS. JOHNSON
text: My name is Pamela Johnson and I’m a landlord.

speaker: MS. JOHNSON
text: My question is, does your party have any future plans to reduce the capital gains tax, especially for retired Americans?

speaker: CLINTON
text: First of all, we have a big plan to reduce the capital gains tax when people sell their homes.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Part of my tax package which is paid for in my balanced budget plan would exempt up to half a million dollars in gains from people when they sell their homes, which I think is the biggest capital gains benefit we could give to most ordinary Americans.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We also have capital gains now for people that invest in new small businesses and hold the investment for five years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It was part of our other economic plan.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And these are things I think that will go a long way toward helping America build a stronger economy and a better tax system.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think the most important thing to emphasize, though, is that we also have to help people in other ways to build a strong economy and we can’t have any tax cut that’s not paid for.

speaker: CLINTON
text: One of the big differences between Senator Dole and myself is that I told you how I’m going to pay for every penny of the tax cuts I recommend and we’ve worked hard to bring this deficit down and that’s helped people in the real estate business because the interest rates are lower.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We’ve got home ownership at a 15-year high.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We’ve got this country going in the right direction.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So we can have a tax cut but my priority would be to help the families who need it with child rearing and education and buying a first-time home and helping for health care costs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So from your business, helping in buying a first-time home, exempting the capital gains on the sale of the home would be the most important things that you asked about.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Thank you, Pamela.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Senator Dole.

speaker: DOLE
text: Pam, what the president didn’t tell you is all his tax cuts expire the year 2000, but these increases go on forever.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’s the liberal approach.

speaker: DOLE
text: You know, give you a little tax cut, give you a couple of years, then make the tax increases go on forever.

speaker: DOLE
text: So the net tax increase in his plan’s somewhere between 60 and 80 billion dollars.

speaker: DOLE
text: We have in the Dole-Kemp economic plan, unless unless your home’s worth over 500,000 dollars.

speaker: DOLE
text: And if it is, I appreciate it congratulate you.

speaker: DOLE
text: But in any event, no tax.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s a good idea, they saw it, they picked it up and put it in theirs, but it’s only temporary.

speaker: DOLE
text: Ours are permanent, ours is a good plan.

speaker: DOLE
text: Create jobs and opportunities.

speaker: DOLE
text: Capital gains rate, cut it in half, cut it 28 percent to 14 percent.

speaker: DOLE
text: There are 7 trillion dollars in assets locked up in America.

speaker: DOLE
text: If we cut the capital gains rate, I’m told everyday, I had a letter from a former constituent in Kansas saying I want to sell property in California, put it in my business in Kansas, I can’t, because the capital gains rate’s too high.

speaker: DOLE
text: We need to get the economy going.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’ll help social security.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’ll create more jobs.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’ll help people who want to get off welfare.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s the American way.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Before Senator Dole left the Senate, he and Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Gingrich also were recommending that we pass these tax cuts only insofar as we could pay for them.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We all assume that the tax cuts will be permanent.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But we have to prove we can pay for them.

speaker: CLINTON
text: After he left the senate, we abandoned that.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s why most experts say that this tax scheme will blow a huge hole in the deficit, raise interest rates and weaken the economy and that will take away all the benefits of the tax cut with a weaker economy.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s why we have to balance the budget, and I will tell you how I’m going to pay for anything I promise you, line by line.

speaker: CLINTON
text: You should expect that from both of us.

speaker: LEHRER
text: All right.

speaker: LEHRER
text: The next question is for Senator Dole.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes, ma’am.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Right there.

speaker: MS. NAUDIN
text: My name is Melissa Naudin.

speaker: MS. NAUDIN
text: I’m a third-year student at UC, San Diego.

speaker: MS. NAUDIN
text: I just want to say it’s a great honor representing the voices of America.

speaker: MS. NAUDIN
text: My voice, my question is concerning you, Mr.

speaker: MS. NAUDIN
text: Dole.

speaker: MS. NAUDIN
text: All the controversy regarding your age.

speaker: MS. NAUDIN
text: How do you feel you can respond to young voices of America today and tomorrow?

speaker: DOLE
text: Well, I think age is very — you know, wisdom comes from age, experience and intelligence.

speaker: DOLE
text: And if you have some of each — and I have some age, some experience and some intelligence — that adds up to wisdom.

speaker: DOLE
text: I think it also is a strength.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s an advantage.

speaker: DOLE
text: And I have a lot of young people work in my office, work in my campaign.

speaker: DOLE
text: This is about America.

speaker: DOLE
text: This is about, somebody said earlier, one of the first questions, we’re together.

speaker: DOLE
text: It’s one America, one nation.

speaker: DOLE
text: I’m looking at our economic plan because I’m concerned about the future for young people.

speaker: DOLE
text: I’m looking about drugs.

speaker: DOLE
text: The president has been AWOL for four years.

speaker: DOLE
text: I’m looking about crime.

speaker: DOLE
text: He’ll claim credit now for crime going down, but it happens because mayors and governors and others have brought crime down.

speaker: DOLE
text: Rudy Giuliani, Mayor of New York, brought crime down 25 percent just in New York City.

speaker: DOLE
text: Of course the president will take credit for that.

speaker: DOLE
text: My view is we want to find jobs and opportunities and education.

speaker: DOLE
text: This year the Republican Congress, as far as student loans went from 24 billion to 36 billion over the next six years.

speaker: DOLE
text: A 50 percent increase.

speaker: DOLE
text: The highest appropriation.

speaker: DOLE
text: 6 billion dollars for Pell Grants, very, very important.

speaker: DOLE
text: We also raised the amount of each Pell Grant.

speaker: DOLE
text: In our economic plan, the $500 child credit can be used for young people, rolled over and over and over, you, of course not this age, but if you have a child two years old, 7 percent interest would be worth about $18,000 by the time that child was ready for college.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I can only tell you that I don’t think Senator Dole is too old to be president.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s the age of his ideas that I question.

speaker: CLINTON
text: You’re almost not old enough to remember this.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But we tried this before, promising people an election year tax cut that’s not paid for.

speaker: DOLE
text: You tried it last time you ran.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Tell him you can have everything you got.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And so let me just say this.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Did you hear him say that Congress just voted to increase student loans and scholarships?

speaker: CLINTON
text: They did after he left.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The last budget he led cut Pell Grants, cut student loans.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I vetoed it when they shut the government down.

speaker: CLINTON
text: My plan would give students a dollar-for-dollar reduction for the cost of a typical community college tuition.

speaker: CLINTON
text: A $10,000 deduction a year for the cost of college tuition.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We let families save in an IRA, withdraw tax free to pay for the cost of education and it’s all paid for.

speaker: CLINTON
text: My whole administration is about your future.

speaker: CLINTON
text: It’s about what the 21st century is going to be like for you.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I hope you will look at the ideas in it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Thank you.

speaker: DOLE
text: When you don’t have any ideas, I guess you say the other person’s ideas are old.

speaker: DOLE
text: As I said earlier, they don’t have any ideas.

speaker: DOLE
text: Their ideas is to raise taxes and spend more money.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’s the liberal philosophy.

speaker: DOLE
text: That’s what you like, you’ve got a perfect candidate.

speaker: DOLE
text: President Clinton came to California in 1992.

speaker: DOLE
text: He said the centerpiece in my first four years is going to be a middle class tax cut.

speaker: DOLE
text: Now all you got that tax cut, congratulations.

speaker: DOLE
text: Because you got a big tax increase.

speaker: DOLE
text: You got a 265 billion dollar tax increase.

speaker: DOLE
text: And he stands here and says politicians who make promises like that ought to be ignored.

speaker: DOLE
text: Well he made the promise.

speaker: DOLE
text: I keep my word, and you will have a tax cut.

speaker: DOLE
text: It will help you in whatever you’re going to do in the next few years.

speaker: DOLE
text: Thank you.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Next question is for President Clinton and it’s from — yes, ma’am.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Yes.

speaker: MS. SANDERS
text: Hello.

speaker: MS. SANDERS
text: My name is Tressia Sanders.

speaker: MS. SANDERS
text: And my question is, do you feel that America has grown enough and has educated itself enough to totally cut out Affirmative Action?

speaker: CLINTON
text: No, ma’am, I don’t.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I am against quotas.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’m against giving anybody any kind of preference for something they’re not qualified for.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But because I still believe that there is some discrimination and that not everybody has an opportunity to prove they’re qualified, I favor the right kind of Affirmative Action.

speaker: CLINTON
